title: Joining Ideas
overview: Build something longer than a sentence. Point back at an idea without leaving the reader guessing, punctuate however and therefore correctly, and set out several reasons in an order somebody can follow. Concede a point early, hedge only what you cannot support, and put what you want at the top rather than the bottom.
learningPath: The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: two letters compared, a writing guide and a letter of complaint.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Refer back to something without the reader having to guess
Join two ideas with however or therefore, and punctuate it right
Concede one thing and argue for another in the same sentence
Set out several reasons in an order somebody can follow
Say how sure you are, instead of stating everything equally firmly
Write a complaint somebody is likely to read to the end
Sum up somebody else's reasoning more briefly than they gave it
lectureScript:
This unit is about what happens between sentences.
Up to now, almost everything you have learned happens inside one sentence. This is about the joins, and the joins are where a reader is won or lost.
The reading opens with a true and ordinary story. A group wrote two letters about the same problem. The first was ignored and the second was answered in a week.
Nothing in the facts changed. Only the building changed.

The first pattern is about pointing backwards.
You know this, that, these and those for things in front of you. This is my key.
In writing they do something else. They point back at a whole IDEA in the sentence before.
Numbers have fallen for three years. This is not a temporary problem.
That this does not refer to any noun. It refers to the entire previous sentence, and that is how paragraphs hold together.
There is a real danger here, and it is worth taking seriously.
The manager told the supplier that his figures were wrong.
Whose figures? The sentence will not tell you, and no amount of rereading will help.
The fix is not clever. Put the noun back in. Repeating a word is not clumsy writing; making somebody guess is.

The second pattern is the commonest punctuation error in written English, and once you see it you will see it everywhere.
But is a conjunction. However is an adverb. They mean nearly the same thing and they are punctuated completely differently.
The price is good, but the delivery is slow. That comma is correct.
The price is good, however the delivery is slow. That comma is wrong.
It is called a comma splice, and it survives because the sentence reads perfectly smoothly.
The reason is that however is not a joining word at all. It is a signpost, and a signpost cannot hold two things together.
So it needs a full stop, or a semicolon.
There is a test that takes two seconds. Cover the linking word and read the two halves.
If both halves are complete sentences, a comma is not strong enough.
And there is a second sign. An adverb can move. The delivery, however, is slow. The delivery is slow, however.
You cannot do that with but. If the word moves, it is not joining anything.
That same rule covers therefore, moreover, furthermore, nevertheless and consequently. All of them are adverbs. None of them can join.

The third pattern is contrast that stays inside one sentence.
Although, while and whereas take a clause. Although it was expensive, we went ahead.
Despite and in spite of take a noun. Despite the cost, we went ahead.
Swapping those two is the usual error, in both directions. Despite it was expensive is wrong. Although the cost is also wrong.
One thing to notice about while. Level 2 taught it as a time word: while I was cooking, the power went off.
Here it means whereas. Same spelling, different job, and only the sentence tells you which.

The fourth pattern is about showing the reader the shape before they need it.
Level 1 gave you first, next, then and finally, for the steps of a task. An argument is not steps. It is points.
Firstly, secondly, lastly. And if you say firstly, you have promised a lastly. Leaving the list open leaves the reader waiting.
There is one pair worth slowing down for, because swapping them changes what you are accusing somebody of.
Subsequently means afterwards, in time. Consequently means as a result.
The part was replaced. Subsequently it failed. That says the failure came later.
The part was replaced. Consequently it failed. That says the repair caused the failure.
Those are very different sentences to put in a letter.

The last pattern is short, and it changes how you sound more than anything else here.
Admittedly. Arguably. Indeed. Notably.
These words carry no information. They tell the reader how much weight to put on what you are saying.
Two moves are worth having.
The first is conceding. Admittedly the evidence is thin, but it is worth checking.
Giving ground early makes everything after it harder to dismiss, and it usually costs nothing.
The letter in the reading does exactly that. It admits that access was difficult, and then adds that three of the four repairs did not need access at all.
The second is hedging, and the judgement is what matters.
Hedge a claim you cannot support. Do not hedge one you can.
If you have the maintenance record, write the part failed on the fourteenth. Writing arguably there gives away ground you did not have to give.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

words.meaning: In addition to what has just been said.
words.example: The cost is high. Furthermore, the delay is unacceptable.
practice: Furthermore starts a new sentence and takes a comma.
It is formal: in speech you would say and another thing.
It adds a SECOND reason, not a detail of the first.
Furthermore and moreover are almost interchangeable.
words.tutor: Add a second reason with furthermore. Ask the tutor whether it was a new point or the same one.

words.meaning: In addition, and this matters too.
words.example: The route is longer. Moreover, it costs more.
practice: Moreover carries slightly more weight than furthermore.
It also starts its own sentence, with a comma after it.
Use it for the point you want remembered.
It is formal and rare in conversation.
words.tutor: Use moreover for the point you most want remembered. Ask the tutor whether it landed.

words.meaning: In any case; and there is another thing.
words.example: It is too expensive. Besides, we do not need it.
practice: Besides is the informal member of this group.
It often introduces the reason that really decides it.
Besides can also be a preposition: besides the cost.
Do not confuse it with beside, which means next to.
words.tutor: Use besides to add the reason that really decides it. Ask the tutor about besides and beside.

words.meaning: As well as that.
words.example: Additionally, the guarantee has expired.
practice: Additionally is neutral and very common in reports.
It starts a sentence and takes a comma.
In addition means the same and is slightly lighter.
It comes from addition, from add.
words.tutor: Add a point with additionally. Ask the tutor whether the register suited the sentence.

words.meaning: In the same way; the same is true of this.
words.example: The first batch failed. Likewise, the second.
practice: Likewise says the same thing happened again.
It is not simply and: it claims a parallel.
Likewise alone can mean me too.
It is one word, not two.
words.tutor: Use likewise to claim a parallel. Ask the tutor whether the two cases really matched.

words.meaning: In a similar way.
words.example: Similarly, the southern route was closed.
practice: Similarly draws a comparison between two cases.
It is slightly weaker than likewise: alike, not identical.
It starts a sentence and takes a comma.
Its adjective is similar, which takes to.
words.tutor: Draw a comparison with similarly. Ask the tutor whether similarly or likewise was right.

words.meaning: But; despite what has just been said.
words.example: The price is good. However, the delivery is slow.
practice: However is an adverb, not a conjunction like but.
It cannot join two clauses with only a comma.
It takes a full stop or a semicolon in front, and a comma after.
However can also mean in whatever way: however you do it.
words.tutor: Contrast two points with however. Ask the tutor to check the punctuation in front of it.

words.meaning: In spite of that; even so.
words.example: It was expensive. Nevertheless, we went ahead.
practice: Nevertheless concedes the point and then overrides it.
It is stronger than however and more formal.
It is one word, with three parts: never the less.
It usually starts a sentence.
words.tutor: Concede a point and then override it. Ask the tutor whether nevertheless was too strong.

words.meaning: Nevertheless; in spite of that.
words.example: The evidence is thin. Nonetheless, it is worth checking.
practice: Nonetheless and nevertheless mean the same thing.
Nonetheless is very slightly more formal.
It can also go at the end: it is worth checking nonetheless.
It is one word.
words.tutor: Use nonetheless at the end of a sentence. Ask the tutor whether it worked there.

words.meaning: The opposite is also true.
words.example: Cheap parts fail sooner. Conversely, good ones last.
practice: Conversely introduces the mirror image of what you just said.
It is not simply but: the two cases must be opposites.
It is formal and belongs in an argument.
Its noun is the converse.
words.tutor: Give the mirror image of a point with conversely. Ask the tutor whether the two were really opposites.

words.meaning: In spite of; without being stopped by.
words.example: Despite the cost, we went ahead.
practice: Despite is a preposition, so a NOUN follows it.
Despite the delay, not despite it was delayed.
Despite the fact that lets you follow it with a clause.
In spite of means exactly the same, in three words.
words.tutor: Use despite with a noun. Ask the tutor to check you did not put a clause after it.

words.meaning: Without paying attention to it; anyway.
words.example: They went ahead regardless.
practice: Regardless of the cost is the full phrase.
Regardless alone, at the end, means anyway.
Regardless of takes a noun.
Irregardless is not a word in careful English.
words.tutor: Use regardless of with a noun. Ask the tutor to check the word after it.

words.meaning: For that reason; so.
words.example: The part failed. Therefore the guarantee applies.
practice: Therefore is the formal so.
It is an adverb, so it cannot join two clauses alone.
It often appears without a comma after it.
Therefore states a logical result, not a time result.
words.tutor: State a conclusion with therefore. Ask the tutor whether it followed logically.

words.meaning: In this way, and so.
words.example: The line was cut. Thus no signal reached the alarm.
practice: Thus is the most formal member of this group.
It can also mean in this way: it was done thus.
Thus far means so far.
It rarely takes a comma after it.
words.tutor: Use thus to state a result. Ask the tutor whether the register was too formal.

words.meaning: For this reason; from this.
words.example: The road floods. Hence the new drain.
practice: Hence is often followed by a noun, with no verb at all.
Hence the new drain is a complete and correct sentence.
It is formal and slightly old-fashioned.
Henceforth means from now on.
words.tutor: Use hence followed by a noun. Ask the tutor whether the short form was acceptable.

words.meaning: As a result of that.
words.example: The supplier failed. Consequently, the work stopped.
practice: Consequently names a result with a clear cause.
It starts a sentence and usually takes a comma.
It comes from consequence.
It is heavier than so and lighter than therefore.
words.tutor: Name a result with consequently. Ask the tutor whether the cause was clear.

words.meaning: In a way that fits what has just been said.
words.example: Numbers fell. We reduced the order accordingly.
practice: Accordingly means we acted to match the situation.
It is often at the end rather than the start.
It is not simply therefore: it implies an adjustment.
According to means as somebody said, which is different.
words.tutor: Use accordingly at the end of a sentence. Ask the tutor whether an adjustment was implied.

words.meaning: Taking everything together.
words.example: Overall, the year was better than expected.
practice: Overall introduces your final judgement.
It goes at the start, before you sum up.
It is also an adjective: the overall cost.
On balance means much the same thing.
words.tutor: Sum up with overall. Ask the tutor whether the judgement covered everything.

words.meaning: As the first point.
words.example: Firstly, the cost is too high.
practice: Firstly, secondly and thirdly number your points.
First also works, and firstly is slightly more formal.
If you say firstly, finish with lastly or finally.
It always takes a comma.
words.tutor: Open an argument with firstly. Ask the tutor whether you finished the list you started.

words.meaning: At the beginning, before things changed.
words.example: Initially we agreed. Later we changed our minds.
practice: Initially describes a first stage that did not last.
Firstly numbers a point; initially describes a time.
It often sets up a later contrast.
It comes from initial.
words.tutor: Set up a contrast with initially. Ask the tutor whether initially or firstly was right.

words.meaning: Afterwards; later than that.
words.example: The part was replaced. Subsequently it failed again.
practice: Subsequently is the formal afterwards.
It describes a sequence in time.
Subsequent is the adjective: a subsequent inspection.
It does not mean as a result: that is consequently.
words.tutor: Describe a sequence with subsequently. Ask the tutor to check it was time, not cause.

words.meaning: In the end, when everything had played out.
words.example: Ultimately the decision was not ours.
practice: Ultimately introduces the final outcome or the real point.
It is stronger than finally: it implies everything considered.
It can start or sit inside a sentence.
Its adjective is ultimate.
words.tutor: State a final outcome with ultimately. Ask the tutor whether it carried enough weight.

words.meaning: After that time, from then on.
words.example: The rule changed in March. Thereafter all applications were checked.
practice: Thereafter means from that point onwards.
It is formal and common in official writing.
It is one word and needs no of.
Shortly thereafter means soon after that.
words.tutor: Use thereafter in a formal sentence. Ask the tutor whether the register matched.

words.meaning: As the final point.
words.example: Lastly, the guarantee has expired.
practice: Lastly closes a list that firstly opened.
Finally means the same and is a little less formal.
Do not use lastly for the last thing that happened in time.
It always takes a comma.
words.tutor: Close an argument with lastly. Ask the tutor whether the list was complete.

words.meaning: It is true that, and I am conceding it.
words.example: Admittedly the evidence is thin.
practice: Admittedly concedes a point before you argue on.
It makes you sound fairer, not weaker.
It usually starts the sentence.
It comes from admit.
words.tutor: Concede a point with admittedly, then argue on. Ask the tutor whether you sounded fairer.

words.meaning: It can be argued that, though not everybody would.
words.example: It is arguably the best of the three.
practice: Arguably marks a claim as open to argument.
It protects you from stating an opinion as a fact.
It goes before the thing being claimed.
It comes from argue.
words.tutor: Make a claim with arguably. Ask the tutor whether it sounded hedged or evasive.

words.meaning: Yes, and more strongly than that.
words.example: The cost is high. Indeed, it has doubled.
practice: Indeed strengthens what you just said.
It often introduces the sharper version of the same point.
It can also mean really: it was indeed broken.
It is not a contrast word.
words.tutor: Strengthen a point with indeed. Ask the tutor whether the second half was stronger.

words.meaning: In particular, and worth noticing.
words.example: Several parts failed, notably the seal.
practice: Notably picks one example out as the important one.
It comes from notable, meaning worth noticing.
It usually sits mid-sentence with a comma.
Most notably is the common strengthener.
words.tutor: Pick out one example with notably. Ask the tutor whether the example earned its place.

words.meaning: Especially; more than the others.
words.example: The winter was hard, particularly in February.
practice: Particularly narrows a general claim to one case.
It is the everyday word for notably.
Not particularly means not very.
It comes from particular.
words.tutor: Narrow a claim with particularly. Ask the tutor whether particularly or notably fitted.

grammar.title: This means that: pointing back at what you just said
grammar.explanation:
You know this, that, these and those for objects in the room.
This is my key. That one is hers.
In an argument they do a different job. They point back at a whole IDEA in
the sentence before, and that is how a paragraph holds together.
grammar.rule:
Pointing at an idea, not a thing:
Numbers have fallen for three years. This is not a temporary problem.
They closed the site with no notice. That is what people object to.
Two suppliers raised their prices. Both of these were long-standing.

The useful frames:
This means that ...     That is why ...
This is the reason ...  That said, ...
Such a change would ... (such points back at a described thing)

THE FORMER and THE LATTER pick out one of exactly two:
We looked at steel and plastic. The former lasts; the latter is cheaper.

ONE and ONES avoid repeating a noun:
The cheap parts failed. The expensive ones did not.

The danger, and it is a real one: what does this refer to?
The manager told the supplier that HIS figures were wrong.
Whose figures? The sentence will not say. Rewrite it, do not hope.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Join these without repeating anything: Numbers have fallen for three years.
It is not a temporary problem.
1. What does the second sentence refer to? The whole first sentence.
2. A whole idea takes this or that, not it.
3. This is right, because the idea is close and still in view.
Answer: Numbers have fallen for three years. This is not a temporary problem.
It is not a temporary problem would be weaker: it points at a noun, and there is no noun to point at.
grammar.mistake:
An ambiguous this or his costs the reader more than a repeated noun does.
Unclear: The manager told the supplier that his figures were wrong.
Clear: The manager told the supplier that the supplier's figures were wrong.
If you have to guess, the writer has failed. Repeat the noun.
grammar.tip: this and that point at ideas. it points at things. When in doubt, repeat the noun.
grammar.practice:
Join each pair without repeating the idea.
1. Numbers have fallen for three years. (that fall) is not temporary.
2. They closed the site with no notice. (that closure) is what people object to.
3. We looked at steel and plastic. (steel) lasts; (plastic) is cheaper.
4. The cheap parts failed. The expensive (parts) did not.
Now rewrite each one so the reference is clear.
5. The manager told the supplier that his figures were wrong.
6. She left the report on the desk and it was gone by Monday.
grammar.answers:
1. This is not temporary.  2. That is what people object to.
3. The former lasts; the latter is cheaper.
4. The expensive ones did not.
5. The manager told the supplier that the supplier's figures were wrong.
   (or: ... that his own figures were wrong, if the manager meant his)
6. She left the report on the desk, and the report was gone by Monday.
   (it could mean the desk, which is why the noun goes back in)
4 or more right: good.

grammar.title: However is not but: the word that cannot join two clauses
grammar.explanation:
This is the single commonest punctuation error in written English, and it
is easy to fix once you see why it happens.
But is a conjunction. However is an adverb. They mean nearly the same thing
and they are punctuated completely differently.
grammar.rule:
A CONJUNCTION joins two clauses with a comma:
The price is good, but the delivery is slow.
and, but, or, so, because, although, while

An ADVERB cannot. It needs a full stop or a semicolon:
The price is good. However, the delivery is slow.
The price is good; however, the delivery is slow.
however, therefore, moreover, furthermore, nevertheless, consequently

THE COMMA SPLICE is what happens when you punctuate the adverb as if it
were a conjunction:
WRONG: The price is good, however the delivery is slow.
That is two complete sentences held together by a comma, which a comma
cannot do on its own.

The test: cover the linking word. Are both halves complete sentences?
If yes, you need a full stop or a semicolon, not a comma.

An adverb can also move, which a conjunction never can:
The delivery, however, is slow.
The delivery is slow, however.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Punctuate this: The price is good ___ however ___ the delivery is slow.
1. Cover however. The price is good. The delivery is slow.
2. Both halves are complete sentences.
3. A comma cannot hold two complete sentences together.
4. however is an adverb, so it takes a full stop or a semicolon in front.
Answer: The price is good. However, the delivery is slow.
Or, with a semicolon: The price is good; however, the delivery is slow.
grammar.mistake:
The comma splice looks right because the sentence reads smoothly.
No: It was expensive, however we went ahead.
Yes: It was expensive. However, we went ahead.
Or use a conjunction instead: It was expensive, but we went ahead.
grammar.tip: Cover the joining word. Two complete sentences means a full stop, never a comma.
grammar.practice:
Punctuate each one correctly. Some need a full stop, some a comma.
1. The price is good ___ however ___ the delivery is slow.
2. The price is good ___ but the delivery is slow.
3. The part failed ___ therefore the guarantee applies.
4. It was expensive ___ so we waited.
5. The evidence is thin ___ nonetheless ___ it is worth checking.
Now correct these three.
6. It was expensive, however we went ahead.
7. Numbers fell, therefore we reduced the order.
8. The route is longer, moreover it costs more.
grammar.answers:
1. The price is good. However, the delivery is slow.
2. The price is good, but the delivery is slow.
3. The part failed. Therefore the guarantee applies.
4. It was expensive, so we waited.
5. The evidence is thin. Nonetheless, it is worth checking.
6, 7 and 8 are all comma splices. Replace each comma with a full stop,
or swap the adverb for a conjunction: but, so, and.
Numbers 2 and 4 are the only conjunctions here, and only they take a comma.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: While it is cheaper, it is slower: contrast that does not start a new sentence
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 taught while for TIME: while I was cooking, the power went off.
The same word has a second job, and the two are told apart only by what
the sentence is doing. Here it means whereas, and it contrasts.
grammar.rule:
ALTHOUGH — concedes, then overrides. A clause follows.
Although it was expensive, we went ahead.
We went ahead, although it was expensive.

WHILE — contrasts two things held side by side. A clause follows.
While the first is cheaper, the second lasts longer.
(the TIME meaning is: while I waited, she rang)

WHEREAS — the same as contrasting while, and only contrast. It never means time.
The first is cheaper, whereas the second lasts longer.

DESPITE and IN SPITE OF — a NOUN follows, never a clause.
Despite the cost, we went ahead.
NOT: Despite it was expensive.
To follow them with a clause you must add the fact that:
Despite the fact that it was expensive, we went ahead.

All four are conjunctions or prepositions, so they take a COMMA, not a full
stop. That is what separates them from however and nevertheless.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Join these with despite: It was expensive. We went ahead.
1. despite is a preposition, so a noun has to follow it.
2. It was expensive is a clause, so turn it into a noun: the cost.
3. Put the contrast first and the main clause second.
Answer: Despite the cost, we went ahead.
If you want to keep the clause, use although: Although it was expensive, we went ahead.
grammar.mistake:
despite is followed by a noun, and although by a clause. Swapping them is the usual error.
No: Despite it was expensive, we went ahead.
Yes: Despite the cost, we went ahead.
Yes: Although it was expensive, we went ahead.
grammar.tip: although and while take a clause. despite takes a noun. All of them take a comma.
grammar.practice:
Join each pair with the word in brackets.
1. It was expensive. We went ahead. (although)
2. It was expensive. We went ahead. (despite)
3. The first is cheaper. The second lasts longer. (whereas)
4. The evidence is thin. It is worth checking. (while)
5. The cost was high. The decision stood. (in spite of)
Now correct these.
6. Despite it was expensive, we went ahead.
7. Although the cost, we went ahead.
grammar.answers:
1. Although it was expensive, we went ahead.
2. Despite the cost, we went ahead.
3. The first is cheaper, whereas the second lasts longer.
4. While the evidence is thin, it is worth checking.
5. In spite of the cost, the decision stood.
6. Despite the cost, we went ahead. (despite needs a noun)
7. Although it was expensive, we went ahead. (although needs a clause)
Numbers 6 and 7 are the same error in both directions.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Firstly, subsequently, ultimately: showing the reader the shape
grammar.explanation:
Level 1 gave you first, next, then, after that and finally, for the steps of
a task. An argument needs a different set, because its parts are not steps
in time. They are points, and the reader needs to know how many are coming
and which one is the last.
grammar.rule:
NUMBERING YOUR POINTS — these are about argument, not time:
Firstly, the cost is too high.
Secondly, the delivery is unreliable.
Lastly, the guarantee has expired.
If you open with firstly, you must close with lastly or finally.

TIME, which is a different job:
Initially we agreed.        (a first stage that did not last)
Subsequently it failed.     (afterwards)
Thereafter every one was checked. (from that point on)

THE CONCLUSION:
Overall, the year was better than expected.
Ultimately the decision was not ours.
Ultimately is not just finally: it means everything considered.

Watch the pair that learners swap:
subsequently = afterwards, in time
consequently = as a result, by cause
The part was replaced. Subsequently it failed. (later)
The part failed. Consequently the line stopped. (because of it)
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose: The part was replaced. ___ it failed again.
1. Ask what the link is. Is the failure CAUSED by the replacement, or just later?
2. The text only says it happened afterwards. No cause is claimed.
3. Afterwards in time is subsequently. Caused by is consequently.
Answer: The part was replaced. Subsequently it failed again.
Writing consequently there would accuse the repair of causing the failure,
which is a much bigger claim than you meant to make.
grammar.mistake:
Opening a numbered list and never closing it leaves the reader waiting.
Weak: Firstly, the cost. Secondly, the delay. The guarantee has expired.
Better: Firstly, the cost. Secondly, the delay. Lastly, the guarantee.
If you say firstly, you have promised a lastly.
grammar.tip: firstly and lastly number your points. Initially and subsequently order time. They are not the same set.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right word.
1. The part was replaced. (Subsequently / Consequently) it failed again.
2. The supplier failed. (Subsequently / Consequently) the work stopped.
3. (Firstly / Initially) we agreed, but later we changed our minds.
4. (Firstly / Initially), the cost is too high. Secondly, the delay.
5. (Overall / Thereafter), the year was better than expected.
6. The rule changed in March. (Ultimately / Thereafter) all applications were checked.
Now finish this list properly.
7. Firstly, the cost. Secondly, the delay. ___ , the guarantee.
grammar.answers:
1. Subsequently (later in time, no cause claimed)
2. Consequently (the failure caused the stoppage)
3. Initially (a first stage that changed)
4. Firstly (numbering a point, not a time)
5. Overall (summing up)
6. Thereafter (from that point on)
7. Lastly, or Finally
Numbers 1 and 2 are the pair everybody swaps. Time, or cause.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Admittedly, arguably: saying how firmly you mean it
grammar.explanation:
This card is short and it changes how you sound more than any other in the
unit. These words do not add information. They tell the reader how much
weight to put on the claim you are making, and leaving them out makes
everything you write sound equally certain, which is rarely true.
grammar.rule:
CONCEDING, before you argue on:
Admittedly the evidence is thin, but it is worth checking.
Of course the cost is high. Even so, ...
It is true that ... . However, ...
Conceding first makes the argument that follows harder to dismiss.

HEDGING, so an opinion is not dressed as a fact:
It is arguably the best of the three.
It seems likely that ...
On balance, ...

STRENGTHENING:
Indeed, it has doubled.  (yes, and more sharply than that)
The cost is high — indeed, it has doubled.

NARROWING to the case that matters:
Several parts failed, notably the seal.
The winter was hard, particularly in February.

The judgement to make: a claim you cannot support should be hedged, and a
claim you can support should not be. Hedging everything is its own problem.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You think it is the best of the three, but you cannot prove it. How do you write it?
1. Ask whether you can support the claim. You cannot, fully.
2. An unsupported opinion written as a fact will be challenged.
3. arguably marks it as open to argument without abandoning it.
Answer: It is arguably the best of the three.
If you COULD prove it, arguably would be the wrong choice: it would
give away ground you did not need to give away.
grammar.mistake:
Hedging a claim you can prove weakens you for nothing.
Weak: The part arguably failed on the fourteenth.
Better: The part failed on the fourteenth.
That is a date from a record. Hedge opinions, not facts.
grammar.tip: Hedge what you cannot support. State what you can. Concede early; it costs less than being caught.
grammar.practice:
Choose the best word for each, and be ready to say why.
1. You think it is the best, but cannot prove it. It is ___ the best.
2. You are conceding a weak point before arguing on. ___ the evidence is thin.
3. You want to sharpen what you just said. The cost is high. ___ , it has doubled.
4. One example matters more than the rest. Several parts failed, ___ the seal.
5. You are summing everything up. ___ , the year was better than expected.
Now decide whether each of these should be hedged, and fix the ones that should not be.
6. The part arguably failed on the fourteenth. (you have the record)
7. This is the cheapest option available. (you checked three of about forty)
grammar.answers:
1. arguably  2. Admittedly  3. Indeed  4. notably  5. Overall
6. The part failed on the fourteenth. You have a record, so do not hedge it.
7. This is arguably the cheapest option available. Three of forty does not
   support a flat claim, so it should be hedged.
Numbers 6 and 7 are the whole judgement: hedge what you cannot support, and only that.
5 or more right: good.

readings.title: The Letter That Was Ignored
readings.setting: A tenants' group, told by the person who wrote the second letter
readings.passage:
We wrote twice. The first letter was ignored and the second was answered within a week.
They were about the same problem and the difference was entirely in how they were built.
The first letter listed everything we were angry about, in the order we thought of it.
It was long, it was true, and nothing in it told the reader what to do.
For the second one we did three things.
Firstly, we numbered the points, so the reader could see there were four and not forty.
Secondly, we conceded the one thing they were right about. Admittedly the access had been difficult.
That cost us nothing and it stopped them dismissing the rest.
Lastly, we put what we wanted at the top instead of the bottom.
The tone changed too. The first letter said the repairs are appalling.
The second said the repairs have not been completed, and gave three dates.
One of those is an opinion and the other is checkable, and only one of them is worth answering.
I do not think they read the first letter to the end. I am fairly sure they read all of the second.

readings.title: The Comma That Cannot Hold
readings.setting: A page from a writing guide
readings.passage:
There is one punctuation error that appears more often than all the others together.
It is called a comma splice, and it looks like this.
The price is good, however the delivery is slow.
The sentence reads smoothly, which is exactly why the error survives.
The problem is that however is an adverb, not a conjunction.
But can join two clauses with a comma. However cannot, because it is not a joining word at all.
It is a signpost, and a signpost does not hold two things together.
There is a test that takes two seconds.
Cover the linking word and read the two halves.
If both halves are complete sentences, a comma is not strong enough. You need a full stop or a semicolon.
The same applies to therefore, moreover, nevertheless, furthermore and consequently.
All of them are adverbs. None of them can join.
There is a second sign, which is that an adverb can move and a conjunction cannot.
The delivery, however, is slow. The delivery is slow, however.
You cannot do that with but. If the word moves, it is not joining anything.

readings.title: Letter: Outstanding Repairs, Flat 14
readings.setting: A letter to a housing office
readings.passage:
Dear Ms Adeyemi

Outstanding repairs, Flat 14, Priory Court

I am writing about four repairs that remain outstanding. I would like a date for each by 30 March.

Firstly, the bathroom window has not closed since 3 January. It was reported twice, on 3 and 17 January.
Secondly, the communal light on the second landing has not worked since December.
Thirdly, the boiler was serviced in November but no certificate was issued.
Lastly, the front door lock was replaced and the second key was never provided.

Admittedly access has been difficult on two occasions, and I accept that the visit on 9 February
could not go ahead for that reason. However, three of the four items above do not require access to the flat.

The boiler certificate is the most urgent, as the insurance renewal falls due in April.
Consequently I would ask that this one is dealt with first.

Overall I would rather resolve this directly than take it further. Nevertheless, I should say
that I have kept copies of all four reports.

Yours sincerely
R. Balewa

comprehension.q: What three things did the writers do differently in the second letter?
comprehension.a: They numbered the points, conceded one thing, and put what they wanted at the top.
comprehension.why: Listed as firstly, secondly and lastly in the middle of the text.

comprehension.q: Why did conceding a point make the letter stronger?
comprehension.a: It cost them nothing and stopped the reader dismissing the rest.
comprehension.why: Stated directly after the concession is described.

comprehension.q: 'The repairs are appalling' and 'the repairs have not been completed'. What is the difference?
comprehension.a: The first is an opinion; the second is checkable.
comprehension.why: The text says only one of them is worth answering.

comprehension.q: Why does the writer think the first letter was not read to the end?
comprehension.a: It was long, unordered, and never told the reader what to do.
comprehension.why: Those three faults are named in the fourth line.

comprehension.q: What is the two-second test the article gives?
comprehension.a: Cover the linking word and see whether both halves are complete sentences.
comprehension.why: Given in the middle of the article.

comprehension.q: Why does the article say the comma splice survives?
comprehension.a: Because the sentence reads smoothly, so nothing sounds wrong.

comprehension.q: What is the second sign that a word is an adverb and not a conjunction?
comprehension.a: It can move within the sentence, and a conjunction cannot.
comprehension.why: The last three lines demonstrate it with however and but.

comprehension.q: How many repairs are outstanding, and by when does the writer want dates?
comprehension.a: Four repairs, with a date for each by 30 March.
comprehension.why: Both are in the opening paragraph, which is where the request belongs.

comprehension.q: Which item does the writer want dealt with first, and why?
comprehension.a: The boiler certificate, because the insurance renewal falls due in April.
comprehension.why: Given with as for the reason and consequently for the request.

comprehension.q: The letter concedes that access was difficult, then says 'However, three of the four items do not require access.' Why is that sentence there?
comprehension.a: It stops the concession being used as an excuse for all four items.
comprehension.why: Conceding narrowly and then limiting the concession is the move Reading 1 describes.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Four points, in order
speaking.instructions:
Make a case about something, real or invented: a complaint, a request, a proposal.
Say exactly four points, and number them aloud.
Open with firstly and close with lastly.
A model, so you can hear the shape:
Firstly, the cost has risen twice this year.
Secondly, the delivery has been late on three occasions.
Thirdly, nobody answered the last two emails.
Lastly, the guarantee expires in April.
Tap the mic. Say your four points. Tap again and listen.
Check: did you close the list you opened?
Could a listener tell how many points were coming?
speaking.tutor: Make your four-point case to the tutor and ask whether the shape was clear before the content.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — The pause a full stop makes
speaking.instructions:
However and but are punctuated differently, and they SOUND different too.
A conjunction runs straight on. An adverb has a real pause in front of it.
Listen and repeat. The slash marks show where the voice stops.
The price is good / but the delivery is slow.   (one small break)
The price is good // However / the delivery is slow.  (a full stop, then a comma)
Now these three pairs.
It was expensive, but we went ahead.
It was expensive. However, we went ahead.
Numbers fell, so we reduced the order.
Numbers fell. Therefore we reduced the order.
Tap the mic. Say all the lines. Tap again and listen.
Check: is the pause before However clearly longer than the one before but?
If they sound the same, your writing will make the same mistake.
speaking.tutor: Say the pairs and ask the tutor whether it could hear which version was punctuated with a full stop.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Concede, then argue
speaking.instructions:
For each position, concede one point aloud and then argue on.
Use admittedly, of course or it is true that for the concession,
and however, nevertheless or even so to turn it round.
1. You want a refund, but you did open the box.
2. You want more hours, but you were late twice last month.
3. You want the repair done, but access has been difficult.
4. You think the plan is wrong, but you have not read all of it.
A model for the first one:
Admittedly I did open the box. Even so, the fault was there before I opened it.
Tap the mic. Say all four. Tap again and listen.
Check: did you concede something real, or something trivial?
A concession nobody cares about does not buy you anything.
speaking.tutor: Say your four concessions and ask the tutor whether any of them gave away too much.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Listen: two letters
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Do not read along. Listen twice.
We wrote twice about the same problem and only the second letter was answered.
The first one listed everything we were angry about, in the order we thought of it.
It was long, it was true, and nothing in it told the reader what to do.
In the second we numbered the points, so the reader could see there were four and not forty.
We conceded the one thing they were right about, which cost us nothing.
And we put what we wanted at the top rather than the bottom.
The tone changed as well. The first said the repairs were appalling. The second said they had not been completed, and gave three dates.
Now answer. Tap the mic and say each answer.
1. Which letter was answered?
2. What was wrong with the first letter?
3. Why did numbering the points help?
4. What is the difference between the two ways of describing the repairs?
Tap again and listen to your answers.
Check: 1 the second. 2 long, unordered, and it never said what was wanted.
3 the reader could see there were four points, not forty. 4 one is an opinion, the other is checkable.
speaking.tutor: Summarise what made the second letter work, in three sentences.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Hedge it, or state it
speaking.instructions:
For each claim, decide whether you can support it, then say it aloud in the right form.
If you can support it, state it flatly. If you cannot, hedge it with arguably or it seems.
1. The part failed on the fourteenth. You have the maintenance record.
2. This is the cheapest option. You checked three of about forty.
3. The second route is quicker. You have driven both, many times.
4. Nobody reads the small print. You have never asked anybody.
5. The window has not closed since January. You reported it twice.
Tap the mic. Say all five. Tap again and listen.
Check: 1, 3 and 5 should be stated flatly. 2 and 4 should be hedged.
Hedging a fact you can prove gives away ground for nothing.
speaking.tutor: Say your five claims and ask the tutor whether you hedged anything you could have proved.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Two minutes: make the case
speaking.instructions:
Make a two-minute case for something you want changed, real or invented.
Build it in this order:
what you want, in one sentence, first
three numbered reasons
one concession, conceded early
what you will do if nothing happens
Use at least four connectives from this unit's word groups.
Tap the mic. Speak for two minutes without stopping.
Tap again and listen to the whole thing.
Check: did you say what you wanted before the reasons, or after?
Did you concede anything, and did it cost you?
speaking.tutor: Make your case to the tutor and ask whether the concession strengthened or weakened it.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Punctuate the joins
writing.prompt:
Below are eight pairs of clauses. Join each one with the word in brackets
and punctuate it correctly. Some take a comma; some need a full stop.
a) The price is good. The delivery is slow. (however)
b) The price is good. The delivery is slow. (but)
c) The part failed. The guarantee applies. (therefore)
d) It was expensive. We waited. (so)
e) The evidence is thin. It is worth checking. (nonetheless)
f) It was expensive. We went ahead. (although)
g) The first is cheaper. The second lasts longer. (whereas)
h) The cost was high. We went ahead. (despite)
writing.model:
a) The price is good. However, the delivery is slow.
b) The price is good, but the delivery is slow.
c) The part failed. Therefore the guarantee applies.
d) It was expensive, so we waited.
e) The evidence is thin. Nonetheless, it is worth checking.
f) Although it was expensive, we went ahead.
g) The first is cheaper, whereas the second lasts longer.
h) Despite the cost, we went ahead.
writing.starter: a) The price is good. However, …
writing.length: Eight joined sentences, about 70 to 100 words.
writing.criteria:
The four adverbs (however, therefore, nonetheless) take a full stop or semicolon.
The conjunctions (but, so, although, whereas) take a comma.
despite is followed by a noun, not a clause.
No comma splice anywhere.
writing.support: For each one, cover the linking word and ask whether both halves are complete sentences.
writing.extension: Rewrite (a) two more ways: with a semicolon, and with however in the middle of the second clause.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A four-point letter
writing.prompt:
Write a letter of complaint or request, in the style of Reading 3.
Put what you want in the FIRST paragraph, then four numbered points,
then one concession, then what you will do next.
Invent the situation entirely.
writing.model:
I am writing about four repairs that remain outstanding. I would like a date for each by 30 March.
Firstly, the bathroom window has not closed since 3 January.
Secondly, the communal light has not worked since December.
Thirdly, the boiler was serviced but no certificate was issued.
Lastly, the second door key was never provided.
Admittedly access has been difficult twice. However, three of the four do not require access.
Overall I would rather resolve this directly. Nevertheless, I have kept copies of all four reports.
writing.criteria:
What you want appears in the first paragraph, not the last.
Four numbered points, opened with firstly and closed with lastly.
One concession, followed by a sentence that limits it.
Every point checkable: a date, a number or a document, not an opinion.
writing.support: Write the four points as bare facts first, with a date beside each. Add the connectives afterwards.
writing.extension: Write the two sentences the OTHER side would use to dismiss your letter, then fix whatever let them.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Make the references clear
writing.prompt:
Below are six sentences where a pronoun is doing too much work.
Rewrite each one so a reader cannot misread it.
a) The manager told the supplier that his figures were wrong.
b) She left the report on the desk and it was gone by Monday.
c) We looked at steel and plastic, and it was cheaper.
d) They cancelled the order and sent a letter about it, which annoyed us.
e) The engineer spoke to the tenant before he left.
f) Numbers fell and costs rose, and this was not expected.
writing.model:
a) The manager told the supplier that the supplier's figures were wrong.
b) She left the report on the desk, and the report was gone by Monday.
c) We looked at steel and plastic; the latter was cheaper.
d) They cancelled the order and sent a letter about the cancellation. The letter annoyed us.
e) The engineer spoke to the tenant before the engineer left.
f) Numbers fell and costs rose. Neither of these was expected.
writing.starter: a) The manager told the supplier that …
writing.criteria:
Each rewrite has exactly one possible reading.
At least one uses the former or the latter.
At least one uses this or these to point at a whole idea.
Repeating a noun is allowed and is often the right answer.
writing.support: For each one, write out both possible meanings first. Then write the version that allows only one.
writing.extension: Find a sentence in your own writing where a this could be misread, and fix it.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Hedge exactly as much as you should
writing.prompt:
Below are six claims and what you actually know. Write each one at the right strength.
a) It is the cheapest option. You checked three of about forty.
b) The part failed on the fourteenth. You have the maintenance record.
c) The new system is better. You have used it for two days.
d) The window has not closed since January. You reported it twice.
e) Nobody reads the small print. You have never asked anybody.
f) The second route is quicker. You have driven both many times.
Then write one sentence saying which was hardest to judge, and why.
writing.model:
a) It is arguably the cheapest option, though I have not compared them all.
b) The part failed on the fourteenth.
c) The new system seems better so far, but two days is not long.
d) The window has not closed since January.
e) Few people seem to read the small print.
f) The second route is quicker.

The hardest was (c), because two days is real evidence and not enough of it.
writing.length: Six claims plus one sentence, about 90 to 120 words.
writing.criteria:
b, d and f stated flatly, with no hedge.
a, c and e hedged, each in a different way.
No claim hedged that the evidence supports.
The final sentence names a real difficulty, not a generality.
writing.support: Write the evidence beside each claim first, then decide. The evidence chooses the wording.
writing.extension: Take (e) and write the version you could state flatly. What would you need to have done first?

activities.title: Practice 1 — Point at the idea
activities.instructions:
Join each pair without repeating the words in brackets.
1. Numbers have fallen for three years. (That fall) is not temporary.
2. They closed the site with no notice. (That closure) is what people object to.
3. We looked at steel and plastic. (Steel) lasts; (plastic) is cheaper.
4. The cheap parts failed. The expensive (parts) did not.
5. Numbers fell and costs rose. (Those two things) were not expected.
Now rewrite each one so it has only one possible meaning.
6. The manager told the supplier that his figures were wrong.
7. She left the report on the desk and it was gone by Monday.
8. The engineer spoke to the tenant before he left.
activities.answers:
1. This is not temporary.  2. That is what people object to.
3. The former lasts; the latter is cheaper.
4. The expensive ones did not.  5. Neither of these was expected.
6. ... that the supplier's figures were wrong.
7. ... and the report was gone by Monday.
8. ... before the engineer left.
In 6, 7 and 8 the fix is to put the noun back. That is not clumsy; it is clear.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For 6 to 8, write out both meanings before you choose. If you cannot see two, look again.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Comma, or full stop?
activities.instructions:
Punctuate each one. Some take a comma, some need a full stop.
1. The price is good ___ however ___ the delivery is slow.
2. The price is good ___ but the delivery is slow.
3. The part failed ___ therefore the guarantee applies.
4. It was expensive ___ so we waited.
5. The evidence is thin ___ nonetheless ___ it is worth checking.
6. It was expensive ___ although we went ahead.
Now correct these three.
7. It was expensive, however we went ahead.
8. Numbers fell, therefore we reduced the order.
9. The route is longer, moreover it costs more.
activities.answers:
1. good. However, the  2. good, but the  3. failed. Therefore the
4. expensive, so we  5. thin. Nonetheless, it  6. expensive, although we
7, 8 and 9 are comma splices. Replace each comma with a full stop,
or swap the adverb for a conjunction: but, so, and.
Only 2, 4 and 6 use conjunctions, and only they take a comma.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Cover the linking word in each one. If both halves are full sentences, a comma will not do.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Clause, or noun?
activities.instructions:
Join each pair with the word in brackets. Watch whether a clause or a noun follows.
1. It was expensive. We went ahead. (although)
2. It was expensive. We went ahead. (despite)
3. The first is cheaper. The second lasts longer. (whereas)
4. The evidence is thin. It is worth checking. (while)
5. The cost was high. The decision stood. (in spite of)
6. It rained all week. The work finished on time. (despite)
Now correct these.
7. Despite it was expensive, we went ahead.
8. Although the cost, we went ahead.
activities.answers:
1. Although it was expensive, we went ahead.
2. Despite the cost, we went ahead.
3. The first is cheaper, whereas the second lasts longer.
4. While the evidence is thin, it is worth checking.
5. In spite of the cost, the decision stood.
6. Despite the rain, the work finished on time.
7. Despite the cost, we went ahead.  8. Although it was expensive, we went ahead.
For every despite, you had to turn a clause into a noun. That is the work.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the noun version beside each clause first: it was expensive becomes the cost.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Time, or cause?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right word.
1. The part was replaced. (Subsequently / Consequently) it failed again.
2. The supplier failed. (Subsequently / Consequently) the work stopped.
3. (Firstly / Initially) we agreed, but later we changed our minds.
4. (Firstly / Initially), the cost is too high. Secondly, the delay.
5. (Overall / Thereafter), the year was better than expected.
6. The rule changed in March. (Ultimately / Thereafter) all applications were checked.
7. (Ultimately / Subsequently) the decision was not ours to make.
8. Firstly, the cost. Secondly, the delay. ___ , the guarantee.
activities.answers:
1. Subsequently  2. Consequently  3. Initially  4. Firstly
5. Overall  6. Thereafter  7. Ultimately  8. Lastly (or Finally)
1 and 2 are the pair everybody swaps: later in TIME, against caused BY.
Writing consequently in 1 would accuse the repair of causing the failure.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For 1 and 2, ask whether the first event CAUSED the second, or merely came before it.

activities.title: Practice 5 — How firmly do you mean it?
activities.instructions:
Choose the best word, and be ready to say why.
1. You think it is best but cannot prove it. It is ___ the best.
2. You are conceding before arguing on. ___ the evidence is thin.
3. You want to sharpen your point. The cost is high. ___ , it has doubled.
4. One example matters most. Several parts failed, ___ the seal.
5. You are summing up. ___ , the year was better than expected.
6. You want to narrow a general claim. The winter was hard, ___ in February.
Now decide: hedge, or state flatly?
7. The part failed on the fourteenth. (you have the record)
8. This is the cheapest option. (you checked three of forty)
activities.answers:
1. arguably  2. Admittedly  3. Indeed  4. notably  5. Overall  6. particularly
7. State it flatly. You have a record, so a hedge gives away ground for nothing.
8. Hedge it: arguably the cheapest. Three of forty does not support a flat claim.
7 and 8 are the judgement the card is really teaching.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the evidence beside each claim before choosing. The evidence picks the wording.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Rebuild the letter
activities.instructions:
Here is a badly built complaint. Rewrite it properly.
Put the request first, number the points, concede once, and make every point checkable.

'The repairs here are appalling and nobody ever answers. The window is broken
and has been for ages and the light on the landing does not work either and
the boiler was done but we got nothing for it and I am still waiting for a
key. It is not good enough and I want something done about it.'
activities.answers:
Yours will differ. A good version has all five of these.
1. The request is in the first sentence: a date for each of four repairs, by a named day.
2. Four numbered points, opened with firstly and closed with lastly.
3. Every point carries a date, a number or a document, not a judgement.
   'broken for ages' becomes 'has not closed since 3 January, reported twice'.
4. One concession, conceded early, and then limited.
5. Nothing like appalling or not good enough, which cannot be answered.
Score yourself out of five. Four or more: good.
activities.solo: List the four facts first, with a date beside each. Only then write sentences round them.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the letter
activities.instructions:
Answer from Reading 3 only.
1. By what date does the writer want a reply?
2. Which repair is most urgent, and why?
3. How many of the four items need access to the flat?
4. Copy the sentence that concedes a point.
5. Copy the sentence that limits that concession, and name the word that turns it.
6. Find one connective from each of the five word groups in this unit.
activities.answers:
1. 30 March.
2. The boiler certificate, because the insurance renewal falls due in April.
3. One of the four. Three do not.
4. 'Admittedly access has been difficult on two occasions ...'
5. 'However, three of the four items above do not require access to the flat.' The word is However.
6. Adding: none used, which is itself worth noticing. Contrasting: However, Nevertheless.
   Concluding: Consequently, Overall. Ordering: Firstly, Secondly, Thirdly, Lastly.
   Qualifying: Admittedly.
Number 6 is the interesting one: a complaint adds nothing, because every point is separate.
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: Read the letter with a pen and circle every connective before you answer.

quizzes.q: The price is good ___ however, the delivery is slow.
quizzes.why: however is an adverb, not a joining word, so it cannot hold two complete sentences together with a comma. A semicolon would also work.

options: It was expensive, however we went ahead.
It was expensive. However, we went ahead.
It was expensive however, we went ahead.
It was expensive, however, we went ahead.
quizzes.a: It was expensive. However, we went ahead.
quizzes.why: The other three are all comma splices: two complete sentences held together by a comma, which a comma cannot do.
the cost is a noun, and despite is the one of these that takes a noun. Although and whereas need a clause.

quizzes.q: ___ it was expensive, we went ahead.
quizzes.why: It was expensive is a clause. Despite and in spite of need a noun, and nevertheless cannot join at all.

quizzes.q: The part was replaced. ___ it failed again. (no cause is being claimed)
quizzes.why: Subsequently means later in time. The other three all claim the replacement CAUSED the failure, which is a much bigger accusation.

quizzes.q: You open a list with 'Firstly'. How must you close it?
quizzes.why: Firstly promises a numbered list, and the reader waits for the end of it. Overall and ultimately sum up; they do not close a count.

quizzes.q: Numbers have fallen for three years. ___ is not a temporary problem.
quizzes.why: The second sentence points at the whole idea in the first, not at a noun in it. this and that point at ideas; it points at things.

quizzes.q: We looked at steel and plastic. The ___ is cheaper. (you mean plastic)
quizzes.why: The latter means the second of exactly two. The former would mean steel.

quizzes.q: You have the maintenance record showing the date. How should you write it?
options: The part failed on the fourteenth.
The part arguably failed on the fourteenth.
The part seems to have failed on the fourteenth.
It could be said the part failed on the fourteenth.
quizzes.a: The part failed on the fourteenth.
quizzes.why: You can prove it, so hedging gives away ground for nothing. Hedge opinions, not facts you hold records for.

quizzes.q: Which word concedes a point before you argue on?
quizzes.why: Indeed strengthens, notably narrows, and likewise claims a parallel. Only admittedly gives ground, which is what makes the rest harder to dismiss.

quizzes.q: The evidence was thin. ___ , it was worth checking.
quizzes.why: The two halves conflict, so you need a contrast word. The other three all ADD to a point rather than turning against it.

quizzes.q: Which sentence has only one possible meaning?
options: The manager told the supplier that his figures were wrong.
She left the report on the desk and it was gone.
The engineer spoke to the tenant before he left.
The manager told the supplier that the supplier's figures were wrong.
quizzes.a: The manager told the supplier that the supplier's figures were wrong.
quizzes.why: Repeating the noun is not clumsy when a pronoun could point at two different people. The other three each allow two readings.

teacherNotes.note: This unit has one `use` code, 7Us.02, and it is about pronouns. The connective work that fills the rest of the unit is carried by the skill codes 7Wor.02 and 7Wc.02, and by all twenty-nine planned words, every one of which is a connective. Both strands are therefore in the contract; only one is a `use` objective. The plan's pattern list has been rewritten to name all five cards.

Card 1 increments L1 U2 and U8 (demonstratives), L2 U1 and U8 (indefinites) and L2 U15 (each other) — all of which taught pronouns pointing at THINGS. Card 3 increments L2 U18, which taught while as a time word only. Card 4 increments L1 U15, which numbered the steps of a task rather than the points of an argument.

The comma splice is the most persistent error in this unit and it is invisible to the ear, because the sentence reads smoothly either way. Speaking 2 exists to make it audible: the pause before however really is longer, and a learner who can hear it will punctuate it.
subsequently and consequently are swapped constantly, and the swap changes what the writer is alleging. In a complaint or a report it is not a stylistic matter.
Learners hedge everything once they meet arguably, which is as damaging as hedging nothing. Practice 5 items 7 and 8 and Writing 4 exist to make the judgement, not the vocabulary, the lesson.

These twenty-nine words are markedly formal, and several (thus, hence, thereafter) would sound strange in conversation. The practice lines say so word by word. A learner who uses them all in speech will sound stilted, and that is worth naming early rather than correcting later.

Practice 6 is the unit's real test: an unstructured complaint to rebuild. It is marked against five structural criteria rather than against wording, because the unit is about building and not about vocabulary.

selfAssessment.statement: I can point back at a whole idea with this or that.
I can spot a sentence where a pronoun could mean two different people.
I know that however needs a full stop in front of it, and but needs a comma.
I can use the two-second test: cover the joining word and read both halves.
I know that although takes a clause and despite takes a noun.
I can number the points of an argument and close the list I opened.
I can tell subsequently from consequently.
I can hedge a claim I cannot support, and state one I can.

assignment.title: The letter that gets answered
assignment.instructions:
Part one. Write a letter of complaint or request about something invented, in about 180 words.
Put what you want in the first paragraph. Number four points, opening with firstly and closing with lastly.
Concede one real thing, then limit the concession in the next sentence.
Every point must be checkable: a date, a number or a document. Nothing that is only an opinion.
Use at least six connectives, drawn from at least four of the five word groups.
Part two. Read your own letter back and check three things, writing one line on each.
Is there a comma splice anywhere? Could any this, that or his be misread? Did you hedge
anything you could actually prove?
Part three. Write the two sentences the other side would use to dismiss your letter,
then fix whatever in your letter let them.
assignment.submissionType: A written letter and a short self-review
